name: Candida
lede: Candida is a dusty rose-mauve, first recorded in 1925, with no documented link to its Latin namesake.

sections.title: The name
sections.body:
The library records the name in Maerz and Paul's dictionary, first recorded in 1925, on plate 51 C 5, and the swatch sits next to [[mauve]] [1]. Why it was called Candida is undocumented [1].

The Latin word *candida* means bright white, and Paterson notes that candidates for office in Rome wore bright white togas, the toga candida [3]. That is where the word candidate comes from, but the color Candida is not white, so the link is only a word [1][3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Candida appears in 0.09% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, as photographed [2]. It is rarer than 65% of the named colors, and it peaks in the 1900s at 0.4% of that century's paintings, 4.4 times the baseline [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 36% of cases [2]. With only 22 paintings, the numbers are thin [2].
